title: Land of Andalus, Green Land, Greet Us
intro: Abu al-Fadl al-Walid's elegy for al-Andalus is in the metre and rhyme of Ibn Zaydun's famous nuniyya, which it names, and of Shawqi's Andalusian ode. He greets the land and counts what the Arabs left there and in Portugal and Sicily, from palaces and mosques to bridges and gardens; he sets their refinement against the Franks of that time, recalls their conquests, and mourns the loss of al-Andalus after the caliphate: Cordoba and its mosque, Madinat al-Zahra' and the Alhambra, to which he sends the lightning and the rain cloud with his greetings. Then he turns to the Arabs of his own day: he calls for modern arms, rejects the “civilising” the colonisers claim to bring, and speaks to a young North African woman of Andalusian descent, with whom he remembers Ibn Zaydun and Wallada. He goes on to mourn Morocco, Algeria, an old grief renewed in Tripoli, and Tunis, and ends with what the French have done. As the poem circulates on poetry sites, four more lines follow, an appeal to the Prophet, which the reciter leaves out.

translation: Land of Andalus, green land, greet us:
perhaps a breath from the Alhambra will bring us to life.
1.sharh: He greets the land and asks it to greet him back, hoping a breath of spirit from the Alhambra will bring him to life. He opens as the old poets did, by greeting an abandoned home, and hayyina, “greet us”, returns as a rhyme at line 103.

translation: In you the treasures and the precious things remain
of the kings who were driven out and scattered.
2.sharh: The treasures and heirlooms of its kings are still there, though the kings themselves were driven out and scattered. The things have outlived their owners.

translation: From us, peace on the bones within you,
on the graves and the ruins that call us back to youth.
3.sharh: He sends his greeting to the bones, graves and ruins of al-Andalus, which tug at him like a beloved calling a man back to the follies of youth.

translation: We lost you in the days of our wretchedness,
and we love you still, and long for you.
4.sharh: The Arabs lost al-Andalus in their days of misfortune, yet they love it and long for it still. Love outlives the loss, and the poem is that love speaking.

translation: Your dwellings, once so full of life, are desolate,
as if we had never lived in them.
5.sharh: Its dwellings, once full of company, are desolate, as if the Arabs had never lived there. It is the oldest theme of the Arabic elegy for an abandoned home, applied here to a whole country.

translation: We watered them with our tears and our blood,
and in their soil a last breath of life shares our grief.
6.sharh: The Arabs watered the land with their tears and their blood, so a last breath of life still stirs in its soil and shares their grief. The dead of al-Andalus and the living mourn together.

translation: It has gone back to its own people, longing for its young men,
and sung them the songs of love.
7.sharh: The land has gone back to its first people, as a widow goes back to her family, yet it longs for its Arab young men and sings them songs of love. The land is a lover pining for those it lost.

translation: It was ours, then it bowed beneath their swords,
but its present is a trace of our past.
8.sharh: Al-Andalus was the Arabs' until it bowed beneath their enemies' swords, but what stands there today is the trace of the Arab past. Everything that remains bears their mark.

translation: In our days of glory it conceived by us, so our image
is kept in it for ever, a consolation to us.
9.sharh: In the Arabs' days of glory the land conceived by them, so it carries their likeness for ever and consoles them with it. It is a mother whose child has its father's face.

translation: No wonder we breathe in fragrance from its flowers:
we were the ones who filled it with sweet herbs.
10.sharh: No wonder the land gives them fragrance from its flowers: they filled it with sweet herbs. Its scent today comes from what the Arabs planted.

translation: And if we delight in the melodies it repeats,
it learned its songs from us.
11.sharh: If they are moved by the tunes the land still plays, it is because it learned its songs from them. He means the Arab mark on the music of Spain.

translation: It longed for the pure Arabic tongue, and it has kept
words of it in which our meanings show.
12.sharh: The land longs for classical Arabic, and it has kept words of it that still carry the Arabs' meanings: the Arabic words that live on in Spanish and Portuguese.

translation: We remember its blessings, and it remembers us:
the lovers' pledge between us has not been lost.
13.sharh: The Arabs remember the land's kindnesses and the land remembers them, so the lovers' pledge between them has not been lost. The remembering is mutual, as between faithful lovers.

translation: In Portugal and Spain our letters
flourished, and our buildings rose for ages.
14.sharh: In Portugal and Spain, Arab letters flourished and Arab buildings stood for ages. Here begins the roll of what the Arabs achieved there.

translation: And in Sicily the monuments still
weep, now for civilisation, now for glory.
15.sharh: In Sicily the Arab monuments still weep, now for the civilisation they stood for and now for its glory. Sicily, too, was Arab before the Normans took it.

translation: How many palaces and ornamented gardens,
where we gathered the arts in all their kinds.
16.sharh: How many palaces and ornamented gardens the Arabs built, gathering every kind of art in them. A list begins, one kind of building to each line.

translation: How many lofty halls and smooth-walled towers,
by which we made the kingdom firm and safe.
17.sharh: How many lofty halls and smooth-walled towers the Arabs raised to make their kingdom firm and safe. Mumarrad, “smooth”, recalls the palace of glass the Queen of Sheba took for water (Quran 27:44).

translation: How many mosques whose minarets we raised,
from which our glories rose like stars.
18.sharh: How many mosques whose minarets the Arabs raised, from which their glories rose like stars. The minarets are where the stars of their greatness rose.

translation: How many bridges whose arches we built,
arches of triumph over a river that mirrors us.
19.sharh: How many bridges the Arabs arched, triumphal arches over a river that mirrors them still. The bridge is a monument to their victory, and the river keeps their reflection.

translation: That land drew from our civilisation
all that our hands created and bestowed on it.
20.sharh: Spain drew from Arab civilisation all that Arab hands created and bestowed on it. Whatever it built later stood on that gift.

translation: Its treasures came from our crafts,
and our farming made its gardens.
21.sharh: Its treasures came from Arab crafts, and its orchards from Arab farming. Craft and agriculture alike were theirs.

translation: After us it grew barren, and the ruins turned desolate,
yearning for us and weeping that we are far.
22.sharh: After the Arabs left, the land grew barren and its ruins desolate, yearning for them and weeping that they are far away. Tana'ina, “our being apart”, echoes the opening of Ibn Zaydun's nuniyya, whose poet the elegy names at line 98.

translation: In the days when the royal palaces stood high,
the Franks were living in the forests.
23.sharh: When the Arab palaces stood high, the Franks were still living in the forests. He sets Arab refinement against the Europe of that time.

translation: And when we trailed robes of silk,
they went about the markets naked.
24.sharh: When the Arabs trailed silk robes, the Franks went about the markets naked. The contrast answers the coloniser's claim, made later in the poem, to bring civilisation.

translation: We wore the finest striped cloaks,
trailing hems of Yemeni cloth in our finery.
25.sharh: The Arabs wore the finest striped cloaks and trailed the hems of Yemeni cloth for show. A trailing hem was the mark of a proud and wealthy man.

translation: We braided our locks in pride
when we guarded our homes for the sake of our women.
26.sharh: They braided their locks in pride when they guarded their homes for their women's sake. Luxury and valour went together.

translation: We rubbed every kind of perfume into our hair
when we put on our mail and saddled our thoroughbreds.
27.sharh: They rubbed perfume into their long hair even as they put on their mail and saddled their horses. For them, refinement and war were not opposites.

translation: All the gems on our women's breasts
became necklaces that raised the pearl's worth.
28.sharh: Every jewel on the breasts of their women became a necklace that raised the pearl's worth. The gems gained value by being worn by them.

translation: The noblest horses wheeled in our battles,
and when the field was quiet, pranced in our pastures.
29.sharh: The noblest horses wheeled in their battles, and when the field was quiet they pranced in their pastures. Jalat, “wheeled”, and khalat, “pranced”, differ only in the dot of one letter.

translation: They gallop, knowing we are their riders,
and still they carry us up, as we mount them.
30.sharh: The horses gallop knowing their riders, and as the Arabs mount them they lift the Arabs up. Na'luha, “we mount them”, and tu'lina, “they raise us”, come from one root.

translation: Our blows gave the swords more edge,
and our thrusts made the spears supple.
31.sharh: Arab blows made the swords keener and Arab thrusts made the spears more supple. The weapons took their qualities from the men who wielded them.

translation: Who leads the battalions, the processions,
who mounts the pulpits, but the lords among us?
32.sharh: Who led the battalions, the processions and the pulpits, if not lords among the Arabs? They led in war, in state and in speech.

translation: Our poems came from the host on high,
and the Rum took their rhymes from us.
33.sharh: Their poems came from the host on high, and Europe took its rhymes from them. The host on high is the Quran's name for the angels (37:8, 38:69), so their verse was inspiration; the claim is that European rhyme came from Arabic.

translation: They knew no learning but from our schools,
and no horsemanship but from our courses.
34.sharh: Europe learned its science only in Arab schools and its horsemanship only on Arab courses. The poet claims for the Arabs the learning and the chivalry Europe prided itself on.

translation: Our armies trod the highest kingdoms,
and set our horses loose in them like wolves.
35.sharh: Arab armies trod the loftiest kingdoms and let their horses run through them like wolves. Here the conquests beyond al-Andalus begin.

translation: Those steeds, bearing the heroes of battle, crossed
the Pyrenees and swooped like falcons.
36.sharh: Those horses carried their heroes over the Pyrenees and swooped like falcons. He recalls the Arab crossing into France in the eighth century.

translation: In the farthest land of France they left a trace
that time has only made clearer.
37.sharh: In the farthest parts of France the Arab horses left a trace that time has only made clearer. He means the raids into southern France, which reached as far as Poitiers.

translation: Their hooves trod snow as they had trodden
sand, and they forded the deep in our campaigns.
38.sharh: Their hooves trod the snows of the north as they had trodden the sands of the south, and they crossed the sea in Arab campaigns. No ground stopped them.

translation: The sun never rose from its high place
but it saw us striving after our goals.
39.sharh: The sun never rose without finding the Arabs striving after their goals. They never rested from the pursuit of greatness.

translation: Chosroes and Caesar: their armies fled
to the marzuban and the patrician, complaining,
40.sharh: The armies of Chosroes and Caesar fled to their commanders with complaints. He goes back to the first conquests, of Persia and Byzantium.

translation: in the days when the turban put crowns to shame,
from the day of Yarmuk to the day of Hattin,
41.sharh: Those were the days when the Arab turban put royal crowns to shame, from Yarmuk to Hattin. The two battles span the glory from the conquest of Syria to Saladin's defeat of the Crusaders.

translation: and thrones came circling round the throne
when the caliph rose to grant the people safety.
42.sharh: Thrones circled the caliph's throne when he rose to grant the people safety. The kings round him are like pilgrims circling the Kaaba.

translation: After the caliphate, the land of Andalus was lost;
the Arabs kept neither their world nor their faith.
43.sharh: After the caliphate the land of al-Andalus was lost, and the Arabs kept neither their world nor their faith. The fall of the caliphate began the end.

translation: Kingship became a mere claim among their factions,
and they clung, astray, to the bonds of pleasure.
44.sharh: Every faction claimed a crown, and its kings held fast to pleasure, not to power. Kingship had become a word.

translation: Each faction swore allegiance to a king
who found no defence against the Spanish raids.
45.sharh: Each faction swore allegiance to its own king, and none of those kings found any defence against the Spanish raids. Division left them defenceless.

translation: So does a ruler lose the awe he commands,
when the people, in their disorder, multiply their rulers.
46.sharh: So a ruler loses his awe when a people in disorder multiply their rulers. Too many kings means no kingdom.

translation: Judgement and strength are with people while they agree;
when they fall out, they become madmen.
47.sharh: People have judgement and strength while they agree; when they quarrel, they lose their minds. It is a general lesson drawn from the history of al-Andalus.

translation: The shade withdrew from the gardens of al-Andalus,
and the sword broke the kingdom of the complacent.
48.sharh: The Arab shade withdrew from the gardens of al-Andalus, and the sword broke the kingdom of those who slept secure. Their heedlessness was punished.

translation: The dwellings are no longer peopled by those who stayed,
nor do the mosques hold anyone at prayer.
49.sharh: The houses are no longer peopled by any who stayed, and the mosques hold no one at prayer. Homes and worship alike are gone.

translation: You will never come back to us, age of Cordoba,
and how can we weep, when our eyes have run dry?
50.sharh: The age of Cordoba will never return, and they cannot even weep for it, since their eyes have run dry. Grief has outlasted tears.

translation: You withered like a flower, yet your scent still intoxicates us,
and your memory consoles us in our trials.
51.sharh: He speaks to the age of Cordoba as to a flower: it has withered, yet its scent still intoxicates them, and its memory consoles them in their trials.

translation: How great a capital of kingship she was,
and how much learning she taught.
52.sharh: How great a capital Cordoba was for kingship, and how much learning it taught. It was the seat of both power and knowledge.

translation: Of her, her kingdom and her retinue, nothing is left
but traces and phantoms that weep with us.
53.sharh: Of Cordoba, its kingdom and its retinue, nothing is left but traces and phantoms that weep with them. Even the ghosts of the past join the mourning.

translation: And time still tells, among the traces of her splendour,
a story that makes our enemies weep.
54.sharh: Among the traces of Cordoba's splendour, time still tells a story that makes even the Arabs' enemies weep. Its glory moves those who destroyed it.

translation: Where are the kings who governed her, the sons of Marwan,
judges by morning, raiders by evening?
55.sharh: Where are the Umayyad kings who governed it, judges by morning and raiders by evening? Justice at home and war on the frontier filled their days.

translation: Where are the sons of Abbad and their splendour,
the last light in our darkness?
56.sharh: Where are the Abbadids and their splendour, the last light in the Arabs' darkness? The kings of Seville shone just before the party kings fell.

translation: You mosque of Cordoba, humbled now,
do the church bells not remind you of the call to prayer?
57.sharh: He asks the Great Mosque of Cordoba, humbled now, whether the church bells do not remind it of the call to prayer. It was made a cathedral, and bells ring where the call was heard.

translation: The caliph walked among its columns
like a lion moving through his den.
58.sharh: The caliph walked among the mosque's columns like a lion moving through its lair. The forest of columns is the lion's thicket.

translation: If he leaned, the earth leaned with him, trembling;
if he spoke, the heavens said “Amen”.
59.sharh: If the caliph leaned, the earth leaned with him in fear; if he spoke, the heavens said “Amen”. Earth and sky obeyed him.

translation: Traveller whose tracking of the past has become a pilgrimage,
stop at the ruins and ask them of our pleasures.
60.sharh: He speaks to the traveller whose visits to the old sites have become a pilgrimage: stop at the ruins and ask them about the Arabs' pleasures. The tourist has taken the place of the people.

translation: After the good life, the royal palaces lie in ruins,
and their people are far away.
61.sharh: After the good life, the royal palaces lie in ruins and their people are far away. The poem comes back to the ruins.

translation: No beauty there delights the eye,
no fragrance comes to us on the breeze.
62.sharh: No beauty there now delights the eye, and no fragrance comes on the breeze. Everything that pleased the senses has gone.

translation: They became ruins, but what remains
grows lovelier with remembering.
63.sharh: The palaces have become ruins, but what remains grows lovelier with remembering. Memory adds beauty to what time has taken.

translation: The palaces of al-Zahra' are effaced,
and we rebuild them in memory, and they rebuild us.
64.sharh: The palaces of Madinat al-Zahra' are effaced, but the Arabs rebuild them in memory, and the memory rebuilds them in turn. Nabniha, “we build them”, turns into tabnina, “they build us”.

translation: From it the palaces looked down on kingdoms,
and kingship loves to build and to adorn.
65.sharh: From al-Zahra' the palaces looked down on kingdoms, for kingship loves to build and adorn. The second half returns in the next line with one word changed.

translation: Its Abd al-Rahman delighted in its ornaments,
and art loves to build and to adorn.
66.sharh: Its Abd al-Rahman delighted in its ornaments, and art loves to build and adorn. With one word changed, the refrain gives kingship and art the same love of building.

translation: It was the reality of power and might,
and in decay it has become a fancy and a guess.
67.sharh: Al-Zahra' was the reality of power and might, and in decay it has become a fancy and a guess. What was once a city is now known only by conjecture.

translation: The turbans of the glorious Arabs still
stir us, figured on embroidered robes.
68.sharh: The turbans of the Arabs, shown on embroidered robes, still stir them. Bi-l-tamthil may mean figured on cloth, or shown in pictures or on the stage; either way the Arabs survive only as images.

translation: In the prayer niches phantoms appear to us,
and from the pulpits voices call.
69.sharh: Phantoms appear to them in the prayer niches, and voices call from the pulpits. The mosque is still alive with its people's memory.

translation: Lightning, look on palaces whose people have left,
and greet the tombs of heroes who settled there.
70.sharh: He asks the lightning to look on palaces whose people have left, and to greet the tombs of the heroes who settled there. The lightning, like the cloud after it, is sent as a messenger, as in the old odes.

translation: Was the Alhambra so desolate
when you used to watch the throngs of singers,
71.sharh: He asks the lightning whether the Alhambra was this desolate when it used to watch the crowds of singers there. The busy past is set against the empty present.

translation: when cloaks rustled on its marble,
and musk of Darin wafted from it?
72.sharh: Cloaks rustled on the Alhambra's marble then, and the musk of Darin filled the air. Musk brought from far away is the measure of that luxury.

translation: And you, cloud, visit the gardens of Murcia,
and water their flowers, roses and eglantine,
73.sharh: He asks the rain cloud to visit the gardens of Murcia and water their roses and eglantine. The cloud is a second messenger.

translation: and rain at dawn on the palms and the olives,
the mulberry and the vine, the pomegranate and the fig.
74.sharh: And to rain at dawn on the palms and olives, the mulberries and vines, the pomegranates and figs. Naming the trees one by one is an act of love.

translation: Treat kindly the sacred trees, I beg you:
every one of them was planted by our hands.
75.sharh: He asks the cloud to treat those trees kindly, for they are sacred: Arab hands planted every one. The trees are the Arabs' legacy, still growing.

translation: We were kings, and the world was our kingdom:
how did we become wretched slaves?
76.sharh: The Arabs were kings and the world their kingdom; how have they become wretched slaves? Here the poem turns from the past to the present, and muluk, “kings”, and mamalik, “slaves”, share a root.

translation: Our blades were blunted on the necks of our enemies,
and now they have taken even our knives.
77.sharh: Their swords were blunted on their enemies' necks, and now the enemy has taken even their knives. Strength has turned to helplessness.

translation: Our valour in war is no use to us:
from their catapults we meet with grinding mills.
78.sharh: Their courage in war is no use now: their enemies' guns grind them like mills. Modern war is won by weapons, not by valour.

translation: Had we been wise, we would have met their shells
with the like, and held out in our fortresses,
79.sharh: Had they been wise, they would have met the enemy's shells with shells and held out in their fortresses. He calls on the Arabs to take up modern arms; sayasi, “fortresses”, is the Quran's word (33:26).

translation: our army would have grown strong to guard our homes,
our fleet come back to guard our shores,
80.sharh: Their army would have grown strong to guard their homes, and their fleet would have come back to guard their shores. The sentence runs on to its answer in the next line.

translation: and then they would have been angels before our might,
not devils come upon us in our weakness.
81.sharh: Then the enemy would have been angels before their strength, and not devils come upon them in their weakness. The strong are respected and the weak attacked.

translation: We are prisoners in our own land without hope,
the home a prison, and the executioner our governor.
82.sharh: They are prisoners without hope in their own land: home is a prison and the executioner is the governor. He means foreign rule in North Africa.

translation: They built forts, and armed them with cannon
enough to fill the earth with fire and destroy us.
83.sharh: The colonisers built forts and armed them with enough cannon to fill the land with fire and destroy the Arabs. It is the machinery of colonial rule.

translation: After aggression, destruction and massacre,
they said, “You are safe: now submit.”
84.sharh: After aggression, destruction and massacre, the colonisers said, “You are safe: now submit.” Safety offered after a massacre is surrender.

translation: How often they say, “We set up for you
the scales of justice”; yet you have never given full measure.
85.sharh: The colonisers keep saying they set up the scales of justice, and the poet turns on them: you have never given full measure. The phrase recalls the Quran's command to give full measure (7:85).

translation: They ruled as their greed wished,
and made terror among us into contempt.
86.sharh: They ruled as their greed pleased and turned terror into contempt among the Arabs. Tahwil, “terror”, and tahwin, “contempt”, differ by a single letter.

translation: Let us not deceive ourselves with hopes,
while the French prowl through our lands.
87.sharh: Let us not deceive ourselves with hopes while the French prowl through our lands. Promises mean nothing while the conqueror walks the land.

translation: Would they ever allow us, were we angels,
to become their equals one day?
88.sharh: Even if the Arabs became angels, the French would never let them become their equals. The coloniser will not accept equality.

translation: They know no give and take when we are gentle,
and we have no weapon to make our claim feared.
89.sharh: The French know no give and take when the Arabs are gentle, and the Arabs have no weapon to make their claims feared. Without strength there is no bargaining.

translation: If we have no wisdom from the knowledge of our present,
have we no lesson from the ignorance of our past?
90.sharh: If the present has not made them wise, the ignorance of their past should at least be a lesson to them. History is the teacher they have ignored.

translation: We live as our forefathers lived,
and want no civilising from the foreigners.
91.sharh: They live as their forefathers lived and want no civilising from foreigners. He rejects the civilising mission the colonisers claimed.

translation: If they offer manna and quails in humiliation,
we choose, with honour, the fruit of Zaqqum and the pus of Hell.
92.sharh: If the colonisers offer manna and quails at the price of humiliation, they would rather eat the food of Hell with honour. Bitterness with honour is better than plenty with shame.

translation: Maghribi girl, so modest,
so veiled in the veil that guards you,
93.sharh: The poem turns to a young woman of North Africa, modest and protected by her veil.

translation: turn from the foreigner, and keep for yourself an Arab brother
from your cousins, who loves the dark-eyed beauties.
94.sharh: He asks her to turn away from the foreigner and keep herself for an Arab cousin, who loves dark-eyed beauties. Marrying among her own people keeps the Arab line.

translation: What a noble Andalusian your grandfather was
in the days of plenty, and this age makes us wretched.
95.sharh: Her grandfather was a noble Andalusian in the days of plenty, and the present age makes them wretched. Many Andalusians settled in North Africa after the fall.

translation: Take my tears, and give me tears of grief:
long have we sought comfort, and comfort has done no good.
96.sharh: He asks her to take his tears and give him hers: they have long sought comfort, and comfort has done no good. Ta'assi, “seeking comfort”, plays on asa, “grief”.

translation: The memory of happiness has made us weep and kept us waking:
but for love, I would not weep, nor would you.
97.sharh: The memory of happiness has made them weep and kept them awake; but for love, neither would weep. Love of the lost land is the source of their tears.

translation: Ibn Zaydun wept when the nun was his sigh,
and his poetry still makes the stricken weep.
98.sharh: Ibn Zaydun wept in his poem rhyming in nun, and his verse still makes the stricken weep. Nun, the letter, chimes with anna, “a sigh”: the rhyme itself is his sigh.

translation: How often he stirred me, moved me, delighted me,
when you were a dove lamenting in a garden.
99.sharh: Ibn Zaydun's verse has often stirred and delighted the poet, when the girl was like a dove lamenting in a garden. The dove's lament and the old poem move him alike.

translation: And your tears, those strings of pearls, were like
the lines of a nuniyya that tells our complaints.
100.sharh: Her tears, like strings of pearls, were like the verses of a nuniyya that tells their complaints. Ibn Zaydun's lament for his love becomes a lament for al-Andalus.

translation: Wallada drew out his loftiest feelings,
and he made his love immortal in verse.
101.sharh: Wallada drew out Ibn Zaydun's loftiest feelings, and he made his love immortal in verse, sung and written down. Love of a woman became poetry that outlived them both.

translation: That princess gave him her grace,
and he turned it into the melody and longing of his verse.
102.sharh: The princess gave him her grace, and he turned it into the melody and longing of his poems. His poetry was the fruit of her love.

translation: Daughter of my uncle, in kinship we have a claim:
guard your face, and when we visit you, greet us.
103.sharh: He calls the North African girl his cousin: kinship gives them a claim on her. She should guard her face, and greet them when they visit; hayyina, “greet us”, is the rhyme the poem began with.

translation: The night of grief has grown so long I took its stars
for what is left of morning, showing through our darkness.
104.sharh: The night of grief has lasted so long that he took its stars for the last of the morning, glimpsed through the darkness. He clings to any light.

translation: We long for a dawn of blessings, and our oppressor
says the light of dawn would harm us.
105.sharh: They long for a dawn of blessings, and their oppressor tells them the light of dawn would harm them. The coloniser denies them even hope.

translation: Then let us raise the morning of the heart
over the night of calamity: that light will do for us.
106.sharh: Then they will raise the morning of their own hearts over the night of calamity, and that light will be enough. If light is denied them from outside, it can come from within.

translation: Was the loss of our kingdom not misfortune enough,
that the barbarians of Rum should come at us in attack?
107.sharh: The loss of their kingdom was misfortune enough, and now the barbarians of Europe have come to attack them as well. The disaster is doubled.

translation: The enemy fell on us in the land across the strait,
which we had accepted as our exile among misfortunes.
108.sharh: The enemy fell on them in North Africa, across the strait, the land they had accepted as their exile after al-Andalus. Ada, al-ida, udwa and awadi play on one root, and the rhyme word recalls Shawqi's Andalusian ode, which opens “ashbahun awadina”, “our misfortunes are alike”.

translation: There the French have never stopped their cannon
tearing apart the unarmed, terrified Arabs.
109.sharh: There the French cannon have never stopped tearing apart the unarmed, terrified Arabs. He describes the French conquest of North Africa.

translation: In the heart of greater Morocco their commander
holds his court, and they have driven the sultans out.
110.sharh: The French commander holds court in the heart of Morocco, and the sultans have been driven out. The seat of power belongs to the conqueror.

translation: And in Algeria is what makes eyes weep blood
for noble men who fell fighting to the death.
111.sharh: In Algeria is what makes eyes weep blood, for noble men who fell fighting to the death. He means the resistance to French rule.

translation: In Tripoli of the West an old grief
has been renewed for us, and our hopes are lost.
112.sharh: In Tripoli an old grief has been renewed, and their hopes are lost. He means the foreign invasion of Tripoli in his own day.

translation: And here is Tunis the green, weeping,
mourning her sons, generous hosts and fierce lancers.
113.sharh: Tunis the green weeps, mourning her sons, generous hosts and fierce lancers. Mata'im and mata'in, “feeders” and “lancers”, differ by a single letter.

translation: From the French come our affliction and our disaster:
will they go on ruling us as tyrants?
114.sharh: Their affliction and their disaster come from the French, and he asks whether the tyranny will last. The roll of the lands ends in that question.

translation: Red beards with blue eyes have appeared,
an evil omen with which the turns of time strike us.
115.sharh: Red beards and blue eyes have appeared among them, an evil omen that time hurls at them. Blue eyes were an ill omen to the Arabs; the Quran gathers the guilty “blue” on the Day of Judgement (20:102).

translation: May we see no more the blue of their eyes,
nor witness the red of their beards.
116.sharh: He prays never again to see the blue of their eyes or the red of their beards. It is a wish to see the colonisers gone.

translation: How long my grief for a people whose homes
shelter barbarians, heavy and scornful.
117.sharh: How long his grief for a people whose homes now shelter barbarians, heavy on them and scornful of them. Thiqal, “heavy”, against mustakhiffin, “making light of”, sets weight against lightness.

translation: They fought as best they could to defend their honour,
then gave in to oppression, obedient.
118.sharh: They fought as best they could for their honour, then gave in to oppression and obeyed. The resistance was defeated.

translation: They have no defence in their poverty,
and they fight for the accursed French.
119.sharh: In their poverty they have no defence, and they fight for the accursed French. The conquered end up serving the conqueror.

translation: Their enemies have carved their homelands to pieces,
and they have become like cattle driven along.
120.sharh: Their enemies cut their homelands to pieces, and they became like cattle driven along. Division brought humiliation.

translation: This, by my life, is God's wrath or the anger
of the Prophet on the heedless and the idle.
121.sharh: This, he swears, is God's wrath or the Prophet's anger on the heedless and the idle. The disaster is a punishment for heedlessness.

translation: Who would believe that these lost, scattered bands
were once armies that saw the world as their battlefield?
122.sharh: Who would believe that these lost, scattered bands were once armies that took the world for their battlefield? Past and present meet again.

translation: For a time they walked on soft and verdant ground,
and today they walk the desert barefoot.
123.sharh: Once they walked on soft and verdant ground; today they walk the desert barefoot. The contrast returns.

translation: No Tariq strikes the barbarians from close by,
and if we call, no Musa answers.
124.sharh: No Tariq strikes the barbarians from close by, and no Musa answers when they call. Tariq, the name, and yatruqu, “strikes by night”, come from one root.

translation: By force they took musk and fine perfume from us,
and gave us mud and clay in exchange.
125.sharh: By force the colonisers took their musk and fine perfume and gave them mud and clay in return. What was taken is set against what was given.

translation: They took their revenge in the raids they launched,
when they came at us as thieves, taking all.
126.sharh: They took their revenge in their raids, coming as thieves who make everything lawful to themselves. Colonial rule is Europe's revenge for the Arab conquests.

translation: They spread corruption in the land, after drinking
the wine of the taverns and sucking on their cigarettes.
127.sharh: They spread corruption in the land after drinking tavern wine and sucking on cigarettes. For all their talk of civilising, the poem ends by calling them drunkards and thieves.

1.1.3.head: أَندَلُس
1.1.3.meaning: Al-Andalus: the Iberian Peninsula, ruled by Arabs for nearly eight centuries.

1.2.4.head: الحَمراء
1.2.4.meaning: Al-Hamra': the Alhambra, palace of the Nasrid kings of Granada, the last Arab kingdom in Spain.

6.2.3.head: حُشاشَة
6.2.3.meaning: Hushasha: the last breath of life left in a body. The poetry sites have the plural, hushashat.

14.1.2.head: البُرتُغال
14.1.2.meaning: Al-Burtughal: Portugal, the west of the Iberian Peninsula, once part of al-Andalus.

15.1.2.head: صِقِلِّيَة
15.1.2.meaning: Siqilliyya: Sicily, under Arab rule for some two centuries.

22.1.4.head: دِمنَة
22.1.4.meaning: Diman: the traces of abandoned camps.

25.2.4.head: العَصب
25.2.4.meaning: Asb: a Yemeni cloth whose yarn was tied and dyed.

27.2.4.head: مُذَكّي
27.2.4.meaning: Madhaki: horses in their full prime.

33.2.1.head: الرّوم
33.2.1.meaning: Al-Rum: the Byzantines, and by extension the Christian Europeans.

40.1.1.meaning: Kisra: Chosroes, title of the Persian kings.

40.2.1.head: المَرزُبان
40.2.1.meaning: Marzuban: a Persian governor and commander.

40.2.2.head: البِطريق
40.2.2.meaning: Bitriq: a Byzantine patrician, a general.

41.2.3.head: اليَرموك
41.2.3.meaning: Yarmuk: the battle of 15 AH (636 CE) that won Syria for the Muslims.

41.2.6.head: حِطّين
41.2.6.meaning: Hattin: Saladin's victory over the Crusaders in 583 AH (1187 CE).

44.1.5.head: طائِفَة
44.1.5.meaning: Tawa'if: the “factions”, the party kings who divided al-Andalus after the caliphate fell.

50.1.6.head: قُرطُبَة
50.1.6.meaning: Qurtuba: Cordoba, capital of the Umayyad caliphate of al-Andalus.

55.1.3-4.meaning: Banu Marwan: the Umayyads of al-Andalus, from Abd al-Rahman I.

56.1.3.head: عَبّاد
56.1.3.meaning: Banu Abbad: the kings of Seville among the party kings; the last was al-Mu'tamid.

64.1.4.head: الزَّهراء
64.1.4.meaning: Al-Zahra': Madinat al-Zahra', the palace city built by Abd al-Rahman al-Nasir outside Cordoba.

66.1.1-2.head: عَبد الرَّحمَن
66.1.1-2.meaning: Abd al-Rahman al-Nasir, the first ruler of al-Andalus to take the title of caliph.

72.2.5.head: دارين
72.2.5.meaning: Darin: a port of old al-Bahrayn, on the Gulf coast of eastern Arabia, where musk from India was landed.

78.2.2.head: بِرقيل
78.2.2.meaning: Baraqil: pellet-bows, catapults; here, their siege guns.

87.2.2.head: جَوس
87.2.2.meaning: Jaws: prowling through a land, as in the Quran's “they went through the homes” (17:5).

92.2.4.head: زَقّوم
92.2.4.meaning: Zaqqum: the tree of Hell, whose fruit the damned eat.

92.2.5.head: غِسلين
92.2.5.meaning: Ghislin: the washings from the wounds of the damned, their only food in Hell (69:36).

93.1.2.head: مَغرِبِيَّة
93.1.2.meaning: Maghribiyya: a woman of the Maghrib, North Africa west of Egypt.

98.1.2-3.meaning: Ibn Zaydun: the poet of Cordoba, author of the famous nuniyya “Distance has taken the place of our nearness”.

100.2.2.head: نونِيَّة
100.2.2.meaning: Nuniyya: a poem rhyming in nun; here Ibn Zaydun's.

101.1.1.head: وَلّادَة
101.1.1.meaning: Wallada: an Umayyad princess and poet, daughter of the caliph al-Mustakfi, beloved of Ibn Zaydun.

108.1.6.head: عُدوَة
108.1.6.meaning: Udwa: “the far shore”, North Africa across the strait from al-Andalus.

110.1.2.head: مَرّاكُش
110.1.2.meaning: Marrakush: Morocco, then called after its old capital, Marrakesh.

110.2.1.head: دَست
110.2.1.meaning: Dast: the seat of honour, the seat of government.

111.1.2.head: الجَزائِر
111.1.2.meaning: Al-Jaza'ir: Algeria, occupied by France from 1830.

112.1.2-3.meaning: Tarabulus al-Gharb: “Tripoli of the West”, Tripoli in Libya, as against Tripoli in Lebanon.

113.1.2.head: تونُس
113.1.2.meaning: Tunis: Tunisia, called “the green”; a French protectorate from 1881.

124.1.2.meaning: Tariq ibn Ziyad, who led the conquest of al-Andalus in 92 AH (711 CE).

124.2.4.meaning: Musa ibn Nusayr, governor of North Africa, who sent Tariq and followed him.
